data.title: Bitcoin rises over 2% to more than $60,000
data.description: Nov 21 : Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market value, was up by around 2.14 per cent at $60,192.07 at 10:16 a.m. ET (1516 GMT) on Saturday.  On Friday, bitcoin broke below $57,742, the lowest since September 2024.

data.title: South Korea's Lee says speed is vital in AI race on data centre visit
data.description: SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae-myung on Saturday (Nov 21) urged the country to move fast as it competes in the global artificial intelligence (AI) race, as he toured a data centre under construction in the southeastern city of Ulsan. "The whole world is competing right now, and speed is vital," Lee said in a public video of his tour. Data centres are a major source of chip demand, and he hoped the success of the project, built by South Korea's second-largest conglomerate SK Group, would draw further investment from global AI companies, Lee said. SK Group is developing the Ulsan data centre jointly with Amazon Web Services (AWS). The estimated cost is 7 trillion won (US$5.2 billion) until 2029, South Korea's science ministry said last year. Operations are scheduled to begin in the second half of 2027. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won said in September that the capacity under construction was an initial 103 megawatt by 2029, with plans to expand it by nearly 900 megawatts in the future. The group is also planning further partnerships with global technology companies as the project progresses, Chey said. On Saturday, President Lee said AI investment had mainly been concentrated around Seoul, and that the Ulsan project showed regional growth was possible. After being told that about 900 people were working at the site, Lee said advanced facilities were short of construction workers and that ministries needed to consider how to train the workforce for building data centres and AI infrastructure.

data.title: Asian tech back in the firing line as traders track Wall Street rout
data.description: HONG KONG: Asian stock markets struggled to recover from last week's sell-off , with tech firms again in the firing line as investors tracked an eye-watering rout on Wall Street. A healthy bounce in US futures was unable to inspire buying amid fears over the AI trade, the prospect of more Federal Reserve interest rate hikes and tighter regulation under a Democrat-led Congress. Scandal-hit Nvidia characterised the collapse in New York on Friday, plunging 14 per cent and helping to drag the Nasdaq into negative territory for the year.  The index has lost almost a fifth of its value since hitting a record high just last month, with strong earnings from Nvidia and a blockbuster IPO from Claude-creator Anthropic unable to staunch the bloodletting.  The selling continued into Asia, with Seoul diving more than 4 per cent as chip titans SK Hynix and Samsung dropped 4 per cent each. "These are not peripheral players in the AI boom but two of its most important semiconductor suppliers," said SPI Asset Management's Stephen Innes. "Their continued weakness suggests investors are still more interested in reducing exposure than celebrating a few hours of improved sentiment in US futures."The losses have led authorities to introduce measures aimed at minimising the negative impact. Taiwan was making it harder to short stocks, while China made it easier to borrow money to buy them and South Korea eyed a stabilisation fund not used since the global financial crisis. Taipei flickered between gains and losses but Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore, Wellington and Jakarta were all deep in negative territory.  Tokyo was closed for a holiday. Meanwhile, the VIX Index - which is seen as the market's fear gauge - spiked to its highest level since April last year, when Donald Trump unveiled his wide-ranging tariff bazooka. Traders have also been spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely. Fiona Cincotta at Forex.com said "nerves have been showing in the AI trade, amid increased scrutiny over AI capital expenditure, the scale of investment, the returns on those investments and when they might materialise". "Furthermore, the Democrats taking control of Congress, which is expected to slow the AI buildout, combined with expectations of higher rates for longer, are fueling concerns about the sector."

data.title: South Korea vows to stabilise stock market after KOSPI drops 5%
data.description: SEJONG, Nov 23 : South Korea reiterated plans on Monday to stabilise its stock market if needed, as the KOSPI plummeted 5 per cent and Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il projected solid economic growth next year. The benchmark index extended declines as concerns over the AI trade and a broader technology selloff overwhelmed the government's assurances that stabilisation funds would be deployed immediately if conditions worsened. "Given the high impact of external uncertainties, volatility in our stock market has expanded significantly, which is why we addressed the issue. The message we delivered yesterday is that we will decide whether to activate measures depending on market conditions," Lee said at a press conference in Sejong. "Accordingly, we are preparing so that necessary steps tailored to the situation will be implemented at an appropriate time." On Sunday, the authorities said they would deploy market stabilisation funds immediately if conditions deteriorated, after the South Korean benchmark index tumbled to a 10-month low last week. Lee said Asia's fourth-largest economy was maintaining strong momentum and could achieve growth in the upper-3 per cent range if present trends continued. Despite the upbeat baseline outlook, Lee warned that external risks remained severe, citing regulatory uncertainty surrounding the artificial intelligence industry, geopolitical instability and rising global interest rates. He cautioned that volatility in the semiconductor sector could spill over and amplify broader macroeconomic swings. Asked whether South Korea could revise rules related to short-selling, Lee said the government's plan was to place greater emphasis on cracking down on illegal short-selling and strengthening surveillance against unfair trading rather than pursuing additional deregulation. South Korea imposed a blanket short-selling ban in late 2023 to curb market volatility and illegal trading, lifting the 17-month prohibition in March 2025 after launching a centralised detection system.

data.title: South Korea's finance minister sees solid growth next year, flags chip volatility risks
data.description: SEOUL, Nov 23 : South Korea's economy is expected to sustain a solid growth trajectory next year as robust exports and investment gradually spill over into domestic demand, Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il said on Monday. Speaking ahead of a news conference in Sejong, Lee said Asia's fourth-largest economy is currently maintaining strong momentum and could achieve growth in the upper-3 per cent range if present trends continue. He added that consumer inflation is projected to ease next year compared with this year, supported by stabilizing global oil prices, though both upside and downside risks remain. Despite the upbeat baseline outlook, Lee warned that external risks remain severe, citing regulatory uncertainty surrounding the artificial intelligence industry, geopolitical instability and rising global interest rates. He cautioned that volatility in the semiconductor sector could spill over and amplify broader macroeconomic swings.

data.title: SoftBank’s Son explored $1 trillion buyout of SK Hynix, the Information reports
data.description: Nov 20 : SoftBank Group CEO Masayoshi Son recently approached Wall Street institutions about financing a possible trillion-dollar "buyout" of South Korean memory chip company SK Hynix, the Information reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. The Information quoted a SoftBank spokesperson as saying Son was no longer considering such a deal.  “SoftBank explores many opportunities, and this one is no longer under active consideration,” the report said, citing the spokesperson.  SK Hynix said in a statement it has no knowledge of the matter described in the Information report. It added that any foreign acquisition of the company would require prior government approval under Korean law. A SoftBank spokesperson referred to the statement the company gave to the Information, when Reuters sought a comment.

data.title: OpenAI scientist proposes industry AI limits tied to model intelligence metric
data.description: Nov 22 : AI developers should adopt common limits on increasingly powerful models and use "perplexity" as a common metric for measuring AI progress across the industry, OpenAI's chief scientist said on Sunday in a proposal backed by CEO Sam Altman. The proposal detailed by OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki in a blog post was unveiled at a time of growing concern inside and outside the industry about the potential risks of AI's rapidly growing capabilities. "I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone," Pachocki wrote. Pachocki described perplexity as a model intelligence metric concerning how well a model predicts the next token — the basic unit of data — on average, and wrote that lower perplexity means better predictions. Pachocki wrote that AI could help drive fundamental advances in AI training methods as soon as 2027, potentially accelerating progress more quickly than advances in monitoring and safety. Developers should commit to not cross agreed capability thresholds until new monitoring and safety mechanisms are in place, Pachocki said. Pachocki advocated for an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, and defines what milestones must be met before that limit is exceeded. Altman backed the proposal, saying in a post on X that the industry should seek agreement on common limits for AI development. Altman described Pachocki's essay as "the most important thing OpenAI has published in awhile," and said such limits would help ensure safety and control.

data.title: Spacecraft begins orbit of Mercury, with a glitch reported
data.description: Nov 22 : After an eight-year journey, the European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has begun orbiting the solar system's smallest and innermost planet Mercury, though the European Space Agency said on Sunday a glitch has occurred involving its thrusters. Mercury, only slightly larger than Earth's moon, is the least explored of the four planets in the inner solar system, with BepiColombo only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and just the second to orbit it. It is a joint mission of the European Space Agency, or ESA, and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency, or JAXA. ESA confirmed on Saturday that BepiColombo had begun its orbit. In a social media post on Sunday, ESA said the spacecraft had a successful entry into orbit, but during the maneuver, "the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue." "The spacecraft is safe and teams at ESOC (the European Space Operations Centre) are working to understand what happened," ESA said, adding that "updates will be provided on Monday." The robotic spacecraft, launched in 2018, is a composite of ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter, which have different scientific objectives and are due to separate on December 9 and 10. Routine science operations are slated to commence in April. The mission will seek to answer questions about Mercury such as why it has a magnetic field, why ice exists in the polar craters of a sun-scorched planet, and what is the nature of enigmatic depressions called "hollows" on its surface. Mercury's surface looks similar to that of the moon, with numerous impact craters. There are expanses of smooth terrain as well as cliffs, some up to a mile (1.6 km) tall. Mercury is about 60 per cent closer to the sun than Earth. That means that from its surface, the sun appears more than three times as large and seven times as luminous as it does when seen from Earth. Mercury's diameter of 3,032 miles (4,880 km) is less than 40 per cent of Earth's diameter of 7,926 miles (12,753 km).

data.title: US intelligence chief predicts more tech outages as systems undergo upgrades
data.description: WASHINGTON, Nov 22 : Americans should expect more technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems, the top US intelligence official said on Sunday. "And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN's "State of the Union" program. "That is going to happen." Clayton was interviewed on Sunday morning news programs days after President Donald Trump attributed a recent spate of technology failures to upgrades of companies' technology systems. Clayton said the upgrades were necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity as technological advances strain older systems. A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network. Speaking on the ABC program "This Week," Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades. Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course."

data.title: Exclusive-Like SpaceX, Anthropic ran an unusual IPO process, chafing some bankers
data.description: NEW YORK, Nov 22 : For the second time this year, Wall Street bankers and lawyers took home a massive paycheck from a record-setting initial public offering. And for the second time this year, some of them came out of it complaining in private about how the process was riddled with complications and unlike any they had worked on before. With SpaceX’s IPO in June, in which banks earned half a billion dollars in fees, bankers chafed over how tightly the Elon Musk-led company controlled the months-long process and kept financial and other information private, making it hard for advisers to do their jobs.  As Anthropic’s IPO, dubbed internally “Project Lantern”, eclipsed SpaceX on Thursday and bankers took home more than half a billion dollars in fees, several people close to the process listed a litany of problems that had plagued the offering process: a compressed timeline, marred by last-minute changes and delays in sharing financial projections; rushed document approvals; and highly unusual restrictions on bankers and concern about leaks — especially after Reuters reported many details from a draft IPO filing weeks before it was made public. Anthropic, for example, instructed some of its 22 IPO underwriters to limit the number of bankers working on the deal to four, asking the firms to make sure they were senior staff, several people familiar with the matter said. One of the people said the restriction likely came out of fear that information would leak, and that the banks found a way to work around it anyway.  Underlying these complaints is a new power dynamic between technology companies and Wall Street. Companies such as SpaceX, Anthropic — and potentially also OpenAI in the future —  have come to wield enormous power as the transformative potential of artificial intelligence creates a frenzied demand for their shares, and they are wielding it to do things their way. That is upsetting some bankers. But banks and investors appear to have little choice but to play along. “These companies certainly did have some market power to tell underwriters that it’s not going to be business as usual,” said Jay Ritter, a University of Florida professor emeritus who researches IPOs. “But the big Wall Street firms, I suspect, are still going to be doing things as business as usual for all but maybe OpenAI (after these two deals).” Ritter added that both SpaceX and Anthropic had negotiated to pay underwriters nothing on the additional shares sold through the greenshoe option. “I don't think most companies are going to be able to demand zero spread on overallotment shares,” he said. Anthropic, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, the two lead underwriters on the two IPOs, declined to comment. SpaceX and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment. Both SpaceX and Anthropic debuted successfully, raising record amounts of money, and their shares rallied initially. A key part of the underwriters’ job is to market the securities. Thanks to the demand for AI, that was an easy sell — both companies had order books oversubscribed many times over.  After an initial burst in shares, the trajectories of the two big AI firms diverged. SpaceX climbed to a post-listing peak of $201.80 on June 16 before retreating below its $135 IPO price for the first time in mid-July. Anthropic’s shares closed down 8.5 per cent on Friday after a 17 per cent first-day pop, as a dramatic unraveling of the AI trade showed that even a blockbuster listing could not shake the gloom hanging over the sector. UNUSUAL NON-COMPETES AND RESTRICTIONS In the case of SpaceX’s IPO, the people close to the process said Musk’s team dictated terms at every stage. Musk's team told the largest and most powerful US banks — including Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley — how to market SpaceX's stock and to whom. It told some banks the specific order sizes they needed to “fill” — in some cases a few billion dollars — and gave them instructions on what types of investors to bring. Banks signed on to underwrite the IPO without being told what they would be paid, the people said. The underlying current running through Anthropic’s IPO process was what several of the people who spoke to Reuters interpreted as a sense of extreme caution.     Anthropic asked some senior officers at banks working on its IPO to sign legal documents restricting core members of the transaction team from working with rival companies, including OpenAI, Cursor, DeepSeek and Hugging Face, for six months after it went public, according to the people.  Banks routinely manage conflicts and protect client confidentiality. But bankers and lawyers said it is rare for an IPO to impose exclusivity this broad, particularly on individual bankers.  In previous head-to-head IPOs such as those of ridesharing rivals Uber and Lyft, or real estate companies Trulia and Zillow, banks could simply pick a side, in part because the deals were smaller and required fewer banks.  Anthropic, by contrast, needed a broad syndicate to raise the enormous amount of capital it was seeking. That, some of the people said, explained why Anthropic sought to bind individual bankers with these restrictions.  One banker who declined to sign on to the agreement said it was a challenge to find people who could promise not to actively cover or engage with Anthropic’s peers, especially as several of those companies pursue their own initial or secondary offerings.   INFORMATION LEAKS AND LATE NIGHTS  Some of the restrictions were meant to control leaks of information.  Nearly four weeks before Anthropic’s filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, called Form S-1, was made public, Reuters reported on it, revealing details of the company’s financials, risk factors, dealings with other tech companies and other information.  Anthropic also used a product called NetRoadshow to share information, instead of regular PDFs, with most of the banks underwriting the deal.  NetRoadshow logs access details, including information such as who has seen the document and looked at which page. Documents on NetRoadshow also had individual bankers’ names as watermarks.  Leaks continued to surface in the press, but using NetRoadshow complicated bankers' work, including because the platform would not let them save copies of documents, one of the people said. Anthropic planned to file an updated securities filing, called an S-1A, with the SEC with the price range and to launch the marketing on November 10. To do so, it needed to send a draft to all the banks in its syndicate for them to sign off on it. The night before it was to happen, a law firm on the deal sent a PDF to the banks about the sale of shares in Canada. But soon it followed with another email asking them to disregard it, saying it “contains incorrect price range and share information,” according to the email, which was seen by Reuters.   The correct S-1A was then sent via the NetRoadshow platform around 2 a.m. New York time. Banks were told they had several hours to sign off on it before it was filed with the SEC.

data.title: Databricks in early talks to raise funds at $225 billion valuation, WSJ reports
data.description: Nov 20 : Databricks is in early talks to raise several billion dollars in a new round that would value the data and artificial intelligence software company at about $225 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday, citing people familiar with the matter. • The deal talks are ongoing and the terms could still change, the report said • Databricks did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment • Databricks had said in August it raised $5 billion at a $190 billion valuation, highlighting strong investor demand for companies tied to the AI boom • Founded in 2013, Databricks provides software that helps companies store, manage and analyze data, as well as develop AI applications • The company competes with Snowflake and is widely viewed as a candidate for a future stock market listing • The company has previously said that its Lakebase product has exceeded a $100 million revenue run-rate, while its Lakehouse data warehousing business surpassed a $1.5 billion revenue run-rate

data.title: GTCR explores potential takeover of payments firm Global Payments
data.description: Nov 20 : GTCR is exploring a potential takeover of payments processor Global Payments, the private equity group said in a filing on Friday, days after reports that a consortium effort with CD&R was dropped. Shares of Global Payments closed the day 10 per cent higher. It was up about 19 per cent so far in 2026. GTCR is working with other private equity firms to finance the potential deal, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters. GTCR, which holds a 16.35 per cent stake in Global Payments and is the largest shareholder, said no definitive decision has been made. Global Payments did not immediately respond to Reuters request for a comment. Private equity firms CD&R and GTCR had dropped their pursuit of Global Payments as a buyout consortium, Reuters reported earlier this month, citing people familiar with the matter. The report had added that it was possible that CD&R and GTCR will resume the talks with Global Payments at a later date or another buyer for the company may emerge. Atlanta-based Global Payments is one of the world's largest payment processors. It enables merchants to accept card and digital payments and provides software and technology services to businesses. Its market value stood at about $22 billion, as of last close. The company has faced pressure in recent years from slowing growth in some business lines, intensifying competition and investor demands to boost profitability. Bloomberg News reported the potential takeover deal first and said it could value Global Payments at $50 billion, including debt and premium.

data.title: Hackers breached US Department of Agriculture, NBC News reports
data.description: Nov 20 : Hackers this week breached a system that the US Department of Agriculture uses to send payments to farmers, NBC News reported on Friday, citing two former USDA officials with knowledge of the matter. The department notified employees of the incident on Thursday, the former officials told NBC. While the payments database is the known extent of the intrusion so far, the former officials warned that the compromised system could provide a backdoor to more sensitive information, including food safety data and research on animal-borne illnesses, according to the report. It is not known who was responsible. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the USDA, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

data.title: Bitcoin rises after falling to two-year low
data.description: Nov 21 : Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency by market value, rose more than 8 per cent to around $59,952 on Saturday, after sliding to its lowest level in two years earlier in the day.  It briefly crossed $60,000 at around 8:30 a.m. EST (1330 GMT).  Bitcoin had fallen to $55,251.60 earlier in the day, its lowest level in two years, after breaking below $57,742 on Friday for the first time since September 2024 as stretched valuations in artificial intelligence stocks rattled investors and weighed on other risk assets.  Crypto markets have ​been ​shaken in recent sessions by weeks of concern about the profitability of massive AI infrastructure spending, rising borrowing costs, regulatory risks following ​Democrats' win in the US midterm elections and the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. A stronger dollar, higher real yields and greater market volatility have all created headwinds for cryptocurrencies, with bitcoin increasingly moving in tandem with stocks.  US stocks extended their rout on Friday, marking one of their steepest weekly declines since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced "Liberation Day" tariffs. The S&P 500 and the Dow both confirmed corrections after Anthropic's momentous market debut fell flat, exacerbating worries about the AI trade that has driven this year's stock market rally.

data.title: Oracle says OpenAI infrastructure deal is fully funded after final capital raise
data.description: Nov 20 : Oracle said on Friday that its infrastructure contract with OpenAI is fully funded following a final capital raise earlier this month. Shares of Oracle rose as much as 3.3 per cent in after-hours trading. • The comments follow investor scrutiny over the amount of capital Oracle would need to fund its expansion of AI data centers and its growing exposure to OpenAI • Oracle and OpenAI plan to develop 4.5 gigawatts of additional data-center capacity in the US, on top of the initial Stargate site in Abilene, Texas • "The financing we outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options," Oracle said in a post on X • The company also said that its Abilene campus, where OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra was trained, is nearly complete • Its next gigawatt-scale campus in Shackelford County, Texas, is fully permitted, and the handover of Nvidia's next-generation Vera Rubin racks is on track for the coming weeks, Oracle said • Oracle announced a $20 billion capital raise earlier this month, consisting of about $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in debt
